impermissible attempt. More fundamentally, as discussed above, subsection (c)(4) requires the district court not only to determine if
consideration of the Gibbs values provides compelling reasons for a remand, but also to articulate how the circumstances that warrant
declining jurisdiction are exceptional. * * *
LEAVY, CIRCUIT JUDGE, dissenting:
* * *
The district court committed no error unless it relied on an unauthorized ground in exercising its discretion to remand. The court did
not say that it relied on an unauthorized ground nor does the record tell us that it did, unless the majority means to hold that likely jury
confusion or the expenditure of substantial additional judicial time are not exceptional circumstances in which compelling reasons for
declining jurisdiction can be found. The fact that the district court does not interpret the 1990 enactment of section 1367 as restricting the
discretionary factors set forth in Gibbs is of no moment unless we can say that the trial court exceeded its lawful authority wherever it
may be found.
* * *

NOTES AND QUESTIONS
1. Recall that Gibbs stated that pendent jurisdiction “is a doctrine of discretion, not of plaintiff’s right,” p. 356, supra. The Ninth Circuit in the
principal case held that 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c) displaced the Gibbs factors, and so narrowed the district court’s discretion to decline to exercise
supplemental jurisdiction. Does the Ninth Circuit’s approach transform supplemental jurisdiction into a matter of plaintiff’s right? See 13D Wright,
Miller & Freer, Federal Practice and Procedure § 3567.3 (3d ed.). Would it be equally reasonable to hold that the statute codified the Gibbs factors so
that the critical question remains whether the exercise of supplemental jurisdiction promotes convenience, fairness, and judicial economy?
Alternatively, could the statute be read as channeling the court’s discretion in light of the policies announced in Gibbs? See Enochs v. Lampasas
County, 641 F.3d 155, 159 (5th Cir. 2011) (stating that courts should “look to the statutory factors set forth by 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c), and to the common
law factors of judicial economy, convenience, fairness, and comity” and then “consider and balance each of the factors”). The Supreme Court has not
yet decided this question.
